summary: OLSRv2 can assign metrics to links and use them to route by more than the fewest hops. This informational document provides a historic record of the rationale and design considerations behind how link metrics were included.

eli5.summary: Sometimes the shortest road is not the best one. This is the diary explaining why the designers let routes use link quality, not just hop count.

questions: why does olsrv2 use link metrics
subtitle: Why OLSRv2 routes by link quality instead of hop count, and the design choices behind its metrics.

tldr.problem: Routing by the fewest hops can pick poor routes in a mobile ad hoc network, for example over weak links or through a relay that should be used only when needed.
tldr.mechanism: OLSRv2 gives each link a dimensionless, additive, directional metric that the receiving router defines, reports it in HELLO and TC messages, and uses two separate sets of multipoint relays, one for flooding and one for routing.
tldr.outcome: This record of design reasoning prescribes no behavior itself. It explains why metrics are built into OLSRv2 from the start, and notes that they cost extra routing MPRs and messages.

today: RFC 7185 is an Informational RFC published in April 2014, and its metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It explains choices in OLSRv2, which is specified in RFC 7181, and does not define behavior itself.

sections.title: Why Hop Count Is Not Enough
sections.content:
OLSRv1 finds routes with the minimum number of hops, and the RFC notes this can give inferior routes in practice. OLSRv2 adds the ability to choose routes using other link metrics. This document is a record of the reasoning, not a specification: it "does not prescribe any behavior".

Metrics were made part of OLSRv2 itself rather than an extension. A router that ignored an extension would still count hops while others used metrics, the two would value routes differently, and the result could be routing loops. The RFC gives several scenarios: a good three-link path preferred over a poor two-link one, a few long-range links that should be saved for when they matter, and an aerial relay with links to many routers that should carry traffic only when essential. Link quality in NHDP is a different tool, since it lets a router decline a link, not prefer one link over another.
sections.eli5: The shortest road is not always the best one. Giving each road a score lets the network avoid bumpy or crowded roads, and save a special shortcut for when it is really needed.

sections.title: What a Link Metric Is
sections.content:
OLSRv2 link metrics are dimensionless, additive, directional and specific to a pair of OLSRv2 interfaces. A route's metric is the sum of its link metrics, so a low value means a good link. How a metric relates to delay, loss or data rate is handled outside OLSRv2. The neighbor metric between two routers is the minimum of the link metrics between them, over symmetric links only.

The RFC discusses how to turn real quantities into metrics. Delay is naturally additive. Loss probability is approximately additive when losses are small and independent. Data rate is not additive and is good when high, so it needs a mapping that inverts the order. For example, with three data rates of 2, 5 and 10 Mbit/s, the fourth power of 10 divided by the data rate gives metrics of 625, 16 and 1. All routers in a MANET should use one metric type. Initially only type zero is defined, with no predefined physical meaning.
sections.eli5: Each road gets a cost number, and a trip costs the sum of its roads. Bad roads cost more. The number can be different going one way than coming back.

sections.title: Directional Metrics and Reporting
sections.content:
A key decision was whether each link has one metric or one per direction. Directional metrics are used because the two ends often see a link differently, and a single shared value would have to be agreed on by both ends or looping could occur. The receiving router defines the metric of its incoming links, since it usually has more information, such as received signal strength, interference levels and error-control coding statistics.

HELLO messages report incoming link metrics, incoming neighbor metrics and outgoing neighbor metrics. TC messages report outgoing neighbor metrics, because routers elsewhere learn about a link only from the router that sends over it. A router must pick an incoming metric as soon as it first hears a neighbor, and the RFC says it is probably best to over-estimate when unsure, using MAXIMUM_METRIC if nothing else is known.
sections.eli5: The one who listens is best placed to say how clear the line is, so the listener scores each road. Everyone then tells their neighbors the scores, so far-away routers can plan trips.

sections.title: The 12-Bit Metric Encoding
sections.content:
Metric values are carried in LINK_METRIC TLVs in a compressed, lossy form of 12 bits. Together with 4 flag bits they fill a 2-octet value field. The form is a modified exponent and mantissa: the maximum represented value is close to but under 2^24, so that a route of at most 255 hops has a total metric under 2^32 and fits in 32 bits. The pair of 4 exponent bits and 8 mantissa bits was selected.

The 12 bits represent 256b+a, so two encoded metrics can be compared as unsigned integers in the same order as the full 24-bit values. The four flag bits mark which of four kinds the value is: incoming or outgoing, and link or neighbor metric, in any combination.
sections.eli5: Big numbers are squeezed into a small space, like rounding a long distance to the nearest ten kilometers. The squeezed numbers still sort in the right order.

sections.title: Two Sets of Multipoint Relays
sections.content:
Multipoint relays (MPRs) serve two jobs: optimized flooding and routing. With metrics these need separate sets, flooding MPRs and routing MPRs. Flooding MPR selection can ignore metrics, but metrics can improve it, for instance by choosing the relay with the lower sum of metrics to reach the 2-hop neighbor.

Routing MPRs must provide a minimum-distance 2-hop route to each symmetric 2-hop neighbor, and Appendix A shows this gives lowest-total-metric routes. A router can thin out this set using local HELLO information. The two sets are generally not equal, even with symmetric metrics. The RFC also admits a cost: metrics may force more routing MPRs, and even require some where none were needed, which can mean more and larger messages. Each router can choose its own selection algorithm and still interoperate.
sections.eli5: Some helpers pass news to everyone nearby and others remember the best roads. With road scores, the best news-passers and the best route-helpers are often different people.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: An attacker could create apparently valid messages that carry incorrect link metrics, influencing the choice of routes or in some cases producing routing loops. The RFC calls this a more subtle and likely less effective attack than other forms of invalid message injection, so no significantly new security issues arise from adding metrics. Defenses are the same as in RFC 7181.
sections.eli5: A trickster could write wrong scores on the road signs. That is no easier to get away with than other tricks, and the same guards protect against it.

items.title: Dimensionless
items.text: OLSRv2 does not know whether a value means delay, loss or data rate.

items.title: Additive
items.text: A route metric is the sum of its link metrics; lower is better.

items.title: Directional
items.text: The metric from A to B can differ from B to A.

items.title: Per interface pair
items.text: Each link between two OLSRv2 interfaces has its own metric.
